opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a tension people point out a lot, but I don't think it's really a contradiction. One-shot design is the north star. It's the thing that forces us to be honest about how good our models actually are. If you aim for "we'll get there after ten rounds of wet lab work," you can paper over a lot of model weaknesses with brute-force experimentation. Aiming for one-shot makes you ask, every time, why didn't the first design work, and what does the model not understand?

But the reality of drug discovery is that a molecule isn't done when it binds the target. You've got developability, specificity, immunogenicity, manufacturability, things that are hard to fully capture computationally today. So even if your first-round hit rate is dramatically higher than it used to be, scientists still iterate. They're optimizing many properties at once, and they want tools that fit that workflow.

The way I think about it, those two things reinforce each other. When the model gets closer to one-shot, iteration gets cheaper and faster. Instead of screening huge libraries and doing many cycles, you're testing a handful of designs and doing one or two refinement rounds. And the products we build for iteration feed the research, because every experiment our partners run tells us where the model is still wrong. That's the most valuable signal we can get.

So the research goal sets the ambition, and the product meets scientists where they are today. Over time, the hope is the number of iterations just keeps shrinking until, for more and more problems, the first answer is good enough.

r001.rationale: The response mentions brute-force experimentation and many cycles, but does not attribute drug discovery’s stage-gated waterfall structure to the high cost of experimentation.

r002.rationale: It says higher first-round hit rates and better models make iteration cheaper and faster, with scientists testing designs and refining them in follow-up rounds.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that one-shot design for some drug classes would shift iterative workflows toward harder classes or modalities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I don't actually think those are in tension. I think they're the same bet viewed at two different timescales.

The one-shot thing is a north star. It's the question we ask ourselves to keep the research honest: if you could only run one experiment, could you hand the biologist a handful of molecules and have one of them work? That's what "one-shot" means to us. It's not that nobody ever iterates again, it's that the model has to carry so much of the search that the wet lab stops being the bottleneck. And you don't get there by pretending you're already there. You get there by being extremely iterative on the way.

Because here's the thing about how drug discovery actually happens today. A medicinal chemist or an antibody engineer doesn't design once. They design, they test, they look at the data, they update their intuition, they design again. That loop is where all the real knowledge lives, and almost none of it is written down anywhere. It's in people's heads and in Excel spreadsheets. If you build a product that just emits a static list of candidates and walks away, you've learned nothing about why the ones that failed, failed. You've thrown away the most valuable signal in the whole process.

So the product has to live inside the loop. You generate, the team tests, the results come back, the model gets to see them, and the next round is better. From the user's perspective that's a tool for iterative experimentation. From our perspective, every one of those cycles is training data for the thing that eventually doesn't need the cycles. Every round where the model's picks are a little more right than last time is a step toward the round where you only need one.

And honestly, the one-shot framing changes how you build the iterative product, too. If your goal is just "make round seven slightly better than round six," you optimize for ergonomics and nice-to-have features. If your goal is "collapse the number of rounds," you get obsessed with calibration. Does the model know what it doesn't know? Can it tell you which of these twenty candidates it's genuinely confident about versus which ones are coin flips? That's the stuff that compresses the loop, and you'd never prioritize it if you weren't aiming at one-shot.

So I'd put it this way. Iterative experimentation is the road. One-shot design is where the road goes. We'd be kidding ourselves if we said we were already at the destination, but we'd also be building the wrong thing if we forgot where we were driving.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeated design and testing, but does not attribute a stage-gated waterfall structure to the high cost of experimentation.

r002.rationale: It describes a loop where the team tests generated candidates, returns results to the model, and uses them to improve the next round.

r003.rationale: It presents one-shot design as the destination of iterative workflows, but does not say those workflows would shift toward harder drug classes or modalities.

astra-6.text:
I think those are complementary. One-shot design is the research goal: you specify the properties you want, and the model produces a molecule that meets them. But building toward that doesn’t mean waiting until the model is perfect before making it useful.

Drug discovery is an experimental process. You make a prediction, test it, and learn something. A product can make that loop more productive today, while the research pushes toward needing fewer iterations. And even if you could design a molecule in one shot, you’d still want to validate it experimentally.

There’s also a distinction between getting the design right and knowing what to ask for. You might successfully design against a particular target and then learn that you need different properties. So the ambition is to take unnecessary trial and error out of molecular design, while giving scientists room to iterate on the underlying scientific question.

r002.rationale: It describes a prediction-test-learn loop and says a product can make that loop more productive, but does not state that models producing promising candidates enable drug discovery to operate iteratively.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that one-shot design for some drug classes would shift iterative workflows toward harder drug classes or modalities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of one-shot design as the research goal, and iteration as how we get there. Ideally, you describe the properties you want in a molecule, we generate a design, and it works when you test it. But making that reliable requires a lot of learning from experiments.

So the product needs to be useful along that path. A scientist should be able to generate candidates, test them, understand what worked, and use that information to guide the next round. Even if we haven’t eliminated iteration, reducing the number of rounds or improving the quality of each round is valuable.

And drug discovery has multiple layers of iteration. Getting a molecule to bind its target doesn’t mean you’ve satisfied every other requirement for a drug. One-shot design can become possible for a particular task while the broader discovery process still involves experimentation. The goal is to make each design decision more predictable, while building tools that help scientists with the uncertainty that remains.

r001.rationale: The response discusses experimentation and iterative rounds but does not attribute drug discovery’s stage-gated waterfall structure to experimentation’s high cost.

r002.rationale: It describes generating candidates, testing them, learning what worked, and using that information to guide the next round, clearly conveying an iterative discovery loop.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes one-shot design for a particular task from broader discovery, but does not say iterative workflows would shift toward harder drug classes or modalities.
